The free safety (FS, ringed) has spun down toward the left edge and the strong safety (SS) has rotated to the deep middle; hollow outlines show where they started. The linebackers (W, M) haven't moved. The right end (the 9, ringed) is the player who chased the last three jets (dashed orange).](03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection_files/figure-html/fig-predict-1-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-1}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**No jet sweep. Fake it, and come back right: a bootleg or a quarterback keep to the right, or an outside
run that way.** The free safety's spin has done the job the linebackers usually do: the defense now has
an extra player at the left edge before the play starts, so the jet sweep would run into the cornerback,
the nickel *and* a safety coming downhill. Meanwhile the linebackers stayed home, so a fake to the jet
won't move them either.

The space is on the **right**. The strong safety has left it for the deep middle, and the one defender
whose job is to guard that side against plays coming back, the backside end, has chased the jet three
times in a row. If he chases the fake again, nobody contains the quarterback: fake the jet left and
boot right, with the tight end and the running back releasing to that side (the waggle's descendant).
That is the series idea from the Wing-T section applied to one defender. If the end stays home this time,
the outside run right, into the side the strong safety left, is the safer call.

Compare this with the jet drill in [02-06](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd),
where the linebackers didn't move and *nobody* replaced them at the edge, so the jet was the right
answer. Same linebackers, different safety, opposite call. An offense that runs the jet as an option
(see the jet sweep section) lets the quarterback make the first half of that decision at the snap.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Second-and-4. The offense is in the Wing-T and has run the buck sweep right twice in a row
from this look. Both times, at the snap, the Mike and Will linebackers (ringed) ran hard to the right with
the pulling guards (their paths from those plays are shown in orange). The offense lines up in the same
formation again. What does series football call now, and why?

::: {#cell-fig-predict-2 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 2: same look, third time")
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(d=5.0)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-7.0, 15.5))
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.3), (5.7, 4.4), (5.0, 8.2)], lw=1.4)
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, -2.6), (3.3, 0.2), (3.0, 3.8)], lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, 8.6, 4.6, "last two plays: the\nlinebackers flew to\nthe pulling guards", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 2: the Wing-T look again (wingback WB outside the tight end on the right, halfback H behind the left tackle, fullback F behind the quarterback). Dashed orange arrows show where the two linebackers (ringed) ran on the last two buck sweeps, as soon as they saw the guards pull.](03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection_files/figure-html/fig-predict-2-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-2}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The buck trap: the fullback keeps the ball up the middle.** The first second will look the same as
the sweep: the quarterback reverse-pivots, the halfback runs across, the fullback heads for the middle,
and the far (left) guard pulls toward the right exactly as he did on the sweep. But this time the
fullback has the ball, and the left guard's pull is a short one: he traps the first defensive lineman
past the center, who was left unblocked at the snap, hitting him from the side. The fullback runs
through the gap where that lineman *was*, straight into the space the two linebackers are about to
vacate by chasing the pull. The more the linebackers trust what they saw on the last two plays, the
bigger the hole.

Why not something else? The waggle punishes the *backside end* for chasing, and the drill told you
about the linebackers. A reverse or counter punishes the *whole defense* flowing, and here only the
second level is flowing hard. Series football means picking the member of the series that beats the
specific reaction you saw. On second-and-4 an inside run that only needs four yards is also exactly
the right risk.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** First-and-10. The offense is in a condensed two-tight-end set, this time with X lined up
tight on the *left*, about eight yards from the ball and inside the cornerback. It has run the
crack-toss to the left twice from this look. Both times the cornerback (ringed) read X stepping inside,
yelled "crack!" and came flying up to take the force (his paths are shown in orange), and the tosses
gained 1 yard and lost 2. Same alignment again. You're the offensive coordinator. What do you call, and
what is X's job?

::: {#cell-fig-predict-3 .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.8, 0.0, "R"),
                            O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                            O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -8.6), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 10.5)])
dfn = front(pe=("5", 4.0), pt=("1", 0.7), bt=("3", -2.35), be=("7", -4.2),
            lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, 2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, -1.4, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, -7.0, "S")),
            cb=(-12.4, 12.0), safeties=((11.0, -7.0), (12.0, 6.5)))
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: same look, third time")
p.highlight("X", color=style.THIRD); p.highlight("LCB", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-17.0, 14.0), window=(-8.5, 14.5))
flow(fld, p, [(6.0, -12.4), (2.4, -11.2), (0.8, -9.8)], lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -11.4, "X: inside\nthe corner", color=GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 8.6, -12.6, "last two plays:\ncorner flies up", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 3: a condensed two-tight-end set to the left. X (green ring) is about 8½ yards from the ball, a yard off the line and inside the cornerback (CB, ringed). The Sam linebacker (S) is between the tight end U and X. Dashed orange: the cornerback's reaction on the last two crack-tosses, straight up to the line as soon as X stepped inside.](03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection_files/figure-html/fig-predict-3-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-3}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Fake the crack and throw it over the cornerback, or switch the blocks.** The corner has learned that
X stepping inside means "crack-toss," and he is now reacting to that first step before he knows what
it is. Use it:

- **The pass.** Run the same toss fake. X takes his crack step inside, the corner flies up, and X
  turns upfield behind him. The deep safety on that side is the only defender who can help, and he has
  been watching two tosses too. This is a play-action pass, the family taught in
  [Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).
- **The run.** Keep the toss, but swap jobs. A corner who sprints to the line is the easiest man on
  the field for X to block, because he is running straight at him, so X blocks the corner and the
  puller takes the Sam instead.

Either way the offense is doing to one cornerback what the Wing-T does to a whole defense: his correct
answer to the last play is his wrong answer to this one. The defense's counter-counter is to have the
corner hold his ground for a count and let a safety take the force, which is why you'll see crack
looks answered differently from week to week.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Outside runs are a **race** between the ball and the defense's pursuit. The defense wins it with a
  **force** player (usually the outermost defender near the line) who turns the ball back inside and
  everyone else pursuing fast. Perimeter plays punish
  a slow defense; misdirection punishes a fast one, and each family needs the other.
- Two blocks make outside runs work: the **crack block**, a receiver or wing hitting an inside defender
  from the side (above the waist, by rule), and the **seal block**, walling a defender off rather than
  moving him. Together with a puller replacing the cracking receiver, they make the **crack-toss**.
- The **jet sweep** turns jet motion's running start into a race the defense starts a step behind, and
  pulls the linebackers sideways even when the ball goes elsewhere. **End-arounds** (one exchange) and
  **reverses** (two) send the ball back against the flow and live or die on the backside end, whose
  rule is to stay home and check boot, counter, reverse.
- The **Wing-T** organized all of this as **series football**: the **buck sweep** and the plays that
  look the same for one second and punish each reaction to it (the trap, the **waggle**, the counter),
  with the belly series as a second conversation. Its children are the NFL's jet sweeps, pull sweeps
  and bootlegs.
- **Eye candy** is motion or a fake that holds defenders without blocking them. Half a second is about
  three yards, which is a gap. It works only as long as the motion is sometimes real.
- Receiver runs are rare (under one per team-game) and, on average, much more valuable than running back
  carries, with more lost-yardage plays. They are **constraint plays**: their value comes from the base
  plays they punish, which is why you can't simply run them more.

import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")

    that hits the ground before anyone catches it is incomplete (Rule 8), so a dropped flip is not a fumble. Example: Tyreek
    Hill's 1-yard touchdown on a jet-motion shovel at the Chargers on Sept. 9, 2018 is recorded in the
    play-by-play as "P.Mahomes pass short middle to T.Hill," with the throw 3 yards behind the line
